tasks.title: Traps already paid for while building the resolver — read before touching this code
tasks.detail: 1) jq/rjq rebinds '.' inside a pipe. 'select($t | has(.id))' asks whether $t has a key named by $t.id, not by the entry's id, so it silently matches nothing; and 'if ($map | has(.id))' silently renames nothing. Bind first: '(.id) as $i | ... has($i)'. This produced two separate silent no-ops in one afternoon, each of which looked like working code. 2) plan_register_temp_file records a path and PRINTS NOTHING, so 'x=$(plan_register_temp_file $(mktemp))' yields an empty path; assign first, register second. 3) A merge conflict cannot be faked: the tool reads git index stages :1 base, :2 ours, :3 theirs, so a fixture with hand-written conflict markers exercises none of it. Build real conflicts in throwaway repos. 4) An entry changed on ONE side only is not a divergence - the changed side wins, the way git merges a line one branch edited. Taking ours-first for every id silently DROPPED a theirs-only edit; that was a real data-loss bug my own test caught. A divergence is both sides changing a base entry differently. 5) from_entries keeps the LAST of a repeated id, so any id-keyed comparison under-reports a register that carries duplicates - check soundness separately. 6) test-flag-coverage.sh requires every accepted flag to appear in --help, which is why the confirmation is the CONFIRM environment variable and not a flag. Its 'every flag has a test' check uses grep -w, and '-' is a non-word character, so a flag that is a hyphen-prefix of another (--confirm inside --confirm-cascade) passes without a test of its own.

tasks.title: Implement IN/1 and IN/2 in rjq
tasks.detail: rjq is the mandated register runtime and does not implement jqs IN/1, so every membership test in a register snippet has to be written the long way with index and an explicit binding. That keeps biting, and it fails in the worst direction: rjq reports the error on stderr and exits non-zero, so a snippet that captures only stdout into a findings variable leaves it empty and prints sound. A validation that checked nothing, reading as a pass. The SKILL.md snippets in bug-report and todo were both rewritten off IN/1 for exactly this reason, and it caught me again today in an ad-hoc TODO.json check. It is a trap peculiar to this repo, because the idiom is standard jq and every agent reaches for it by default. jq defines both arities in its own stdlib in terms of any, so this is plausibly a prelude definition rather than Rust work - read the IN definitions in jqs builtin.jq and port them rather than trusting a remembered one-liner. Land it with a test that the register snippets in both SKILL.md files run green under rjq, since that is the whole point of having it, and a test that a membership test against a missing key is false rather than an error. Until it lands, reg_findings in planning/scripts/register-lib.sh is the one place that expression should live and callers should use it instead of hand-rolling.

tasks.title: Give every skill a load sanity check the agent must execute
tasks.detail: Every shipped skill gets a check that proves the agent actually read the whole thing, because the measured truncation is SILENT. Claude Code 2.1.259 returns a prefix at roughly 25,000 tokens with no notice anywhere; opencode 1.18.27 caps an -f attachment at 50 KB but does say so in-band; codex 0.153.0 does not truncate. So on the harness we use most, a skill over the cap is read in part and nothing says so - and an agent asked why content was missing rationalised it as having declined to load repetitive filler, when the transcript showed one unbounded Read handing it 1078 lines. planning/SKILL.md is over the cap today at 1502 lines and 87.8 KB, losing about 35 percent in 2 of 3 real runs. Design, per Michael. First, the sanity token does NOT sit at the end of the file. The end is predictable and a reader that stops early can still be told what to say; place it at a RANDOM position past the known boundary, so its presence is evidence of having read past the cap rather than evidence of having reached a fixed landmark. Past the boundary means past the measured caps above, and random means the position is not guessable from the file shape. Second, loading the skill is not finished by echoing anything: the agent must RUN THE COMMAND WITH THE SANITY ARGUMENTS it can only have obtained by reading that far, and the command is what decides. An instruction to report a token is claimable; an invocation carrying an argument the agent could not otherwise know is not. That distinction is the whole point, and it is why this is worth having as an interlock rather than a line of prose. Scope is all skills, not just planning: the same silent cap applies to any of them that grows, and a check only present on the one file we already know about would not catch the next one. Evidence and the eleven reproducible probes are in .agents/skill-loading-findings.md on this branch. Related: the planning split under discussion (Q11) reuses the existing REVIEWER_SECTION marker plus generate-reviewer.sh plus the hash pinned by test-reviewer-projection.sh, which is already a marked-region-and-generator mechanism, so the split and this check should share it rather than inventing a second scheme.

tasks.title: Split planning/SKILL.md: authored source, generated short SKILL.md
tasks.detail: DECIDED by Michael, 2026-09-03. planning/SKILL.md is 1502 lines and 87.8 KB, over the roughly 25,000-token cap at which Claude Code silently returns a prefix, and it measurably loses about 35 percent of itself in 2 of 3 real runs. The shape: the full authored content becomes a SOURCE file - source.skill or similar, not a .md - and a SHORT SKILL.md is GENERATED from it, carrying the front matter and pointers to generated part files. The non-.md extension is load bearing, not cosmetic: an agent looking for SKILL.md must not stumble into the 1500-line source, which is exactly the failure being fixed. Section sizes make the split obvious - section 3 mandatory classification and independent review is 509 lines, section 2 create the plan directory is 365, section 4 resume and update is 342, and everything else is 286. Three parts and a thin index, each part well under the cap. This repo already has the machinery and the convention: install.sh is generated from installer/src, installer/build.sh has a --check mode that diffs instead of writing, and planning/tests/test-installer-build.sh fails when the committed artifact is stale. Follow that pattern exactly rather than inventing one - a generator, a --check mode, and a test that the committed output matches its source. Consequences to handle, none optional. The generated SKILL.md and the parts stay COMMITTED and SHIPPED, because a skill is consumed as files and has no build step at the far end. MODE markers flip: the source is MODE DEV, the generated outputs are MODE PROD, per contract 10a. generate-reviewer.sh currently projects two REVIEWER_SECTION blocks out of SKILL.md, at lines 650-947 and 1190-1276, 383 lines or 25 percent of the file, and pins the source SHA-256 that test-reviewer-projection.sh compares - it must read the SOURCE after this change, and its recorded hash necessarily changes. skill_files() in installer/src/50-manifest.sh must list the new part files, and the npm baseline rows follow from that. The five never-committed generated plan-*-lib.sh files and REVIEWER.md are the precedent for what setup-dev-env.sh has to build. Finally this interlocks with T86: the load sanity check needs a token at a random position past the cap in each part, so build the split and the check together rather than retrofitting the check afterwards.
tasks.note: Multi-target generation confirmed as the shape (Michael, Q18): one authored source emits SEVERAL documents, not just a short SKILL.md. The existing REVIEWER_SECTION marker already names a region - mandatory-review and bounded-context - so the extension is to have a region declare which target or targets it belongs to, and have one generator emit every target from the single source, with one --check mode diffing all of them and one staleness test covering the set. That subsumes generate-reviewer.sh rather than sitting beside it, and it means a section wanted in two documents is authored once and projected twice, which is the actual answer to sections repeating across documents. Two constraints on it: a region has to carry MODE as well as target, because SKILL.md and its parts ship as PROD while MAINTAINER.md is DEV, and a region projected into two targets must be projected verbatim, since the reviewer projection is pinned by SHA-256. On MAINTAINER.md specifically, 449 lines and 38 KB: it is UNDER the roughly 25,000-token cap, so it does not need splitting to be read whole, and measurement says it shares NOTHING with SKILL.md - comparing every heading across SKILL.md, ROLES.md, MAINTAINER.md, ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/README.md found zero overlap. So it can be a target of the same source, and today that would buy structure rather than deduplication. Worth doing only if the convention of one source per skill is wanted for its own sake; not required by the truncation problem.

tasks.title: a www skill: a brake the human can pull, and one the agent pulls on itself when it is thrashing
tasks.detail:
www is the three W's, and the skill's whole job is to make the agent answer all three, in order, before it does anything else. W1 What do we have? W2 What are the values? W3 What are we trying to achieve? These are Tschallacka's own words and they are the required prompts -- not a paraphrase, not a longer checklist. They earned their place by resolving a thrashing agent immediately, in a short time, where more elaborate prodding had not.

Two triggers, one behaviour. (1) The human types 'www' -- that alone means stop: no further tool calls, no continuing the current line of attack. (2) The agent notices it is thrashing: retrying variants of a failing command, re-reading the same files, guessing at a cause it has not measured, or otherwise acting without knowing. Same brake, pulled by the agent on itself, without waiting to be told.

Answering all three W's is the gate, and each has a distinct job. 'What do we have' forces an inventory of what is actually in hand -- the real error text, the measured facts, the files that exist -- separated from what was assumed. 'What are the values' forces the concrete particulars out into the open: the actual paths, ports, ids, exit codes and settings, rather than the shape of the problem in the abstract, which is where a thrashing agent hides. 'What are we trying to achieve' forces the goal back into view, which is the one a thrashing agent has usually lost while chasing a symptom.

Only after all three are answered may work continue, and then with one reasoned step or a numbered question -- never another speculative attempt. Requested by Tschallacka on 2026-09-04, after a session where a worker guessed three times at a Darwin errno instead of stopping, and where a hypothesis stayed wrongly ruled out for a day because two variables were tested together.

tasks.title: expose the chat client as an MCP server, so joining a channel is a tool call rather than CLI archaeology
tasks.detail:
Today an agent talks to the chat bus by shelling out to chat-client-rs, and that is where it goes wrong: it has to know the binary's path for its platform, the chat home, whether a server is already running, and which subcommand carries which flag. Observed repeatedly on 2026-09-04 -- an agent started a rival server on a second port and split the channel, another reached for --insecure and defeated the cert pinning, and both had to be told the port by hand. That is filed as B124; an MCP is the structural answer to it, where B124's own fix is only better affordance in the CLI.

As an MCP the operations become named tools with typed arguments -- join, send, read since a cursor, list channels, who is here -- and the server resolves discovery, the chat home and the cert itself, so there is no port for a model to guess and no --insecure to reach for. Follow src/ai-text-editor-mcp, which already does this in this repo for the editor: same crate layout, same packaging, same per-skill binary placement, rather than inventing a second pattern.

The liveness point is the reason this is HIGH and not a nicety. Michael's requirement is that the chat stays up and clients stay attached, because a held connection is what makes answers quick -- an agent learns of a message when it arrives instead of on its next poll. A one-shot CLI cannot hold anything: every invocation connects, does one thing and exits, so there is no presence and no push. An in-process MCP server can hold the connection for the life of the session and surface an incoming message as it lands. Note the two things that must be true first: the broadcast path has to be reliable (B122, fixed on PR #43 -- before it, holding a subscriber wedged the whole server), and chat-client-rs today never consumes a broadcast at all, it FETCH-polls and discards PRIVMSG (measured by chat-b122 on #43), so the MCP has to consume broadcasts properly rather than wrap the existing polling.

Requested by Tschallacka on 2026-09-04.

tasks.title: the socket is the only interface to the chat bus: nothing outside the server may touch the channel log
tasks.detail:
Architectural rule set by Tschallacka on 2026-09-04: everything goes over the socket, and nothing interfaces the log. The channel log is the SERVER's private storage format, not an API. Two things follow, and both are violations present today.

(1) No client may read the log file. chat-client-rs has 'read --local' and 'tail --local' which walk $AI_CHAT_HOME/channels/<chan>.log directly with no server, and the docs advertise it. That has to go, or survive only as an explicitly-labelled maintenance escape hatch that no agent instruction ever recommends. pr-master's own coordination poller was reading the log this way as a workaround for B122 -- a live tail wedged the server -- which is exactly the shortcut this rule forbids, and it must move to a socket tail once B122 lands.

(2) Steady-state delivery is a PUSH over the socket, not a poll. Today 'tail' is a loop issuing FETCH <chan> <last_id>, and the client discards broadcast PRIVMSG lines except to confirm its own send echoed -- measured by chat-b122 on PR #43. So the server's whole fan-out path serves stock IRC clients only, while our own client polls. Invert it: the client consumes PRIVMSG as it arrives, so a message reaches an agent when it is sent rather than on the next poll interval. This is the liveness requirement behind wanting the chat up at all -- a held connection is what makes answers quick.

Where FETCH legitimately stays: backfill. On join or reconnect a client asks for what it missed since its cursor, over the SOCKET, and then follows the push stream. That is not log interfacing and not steady-state polling.

Depends on B122 (PR #43): before it, a held subscriber wedged the server, which is why polling was tolerated. Related: B124 (connect affordance) and T90 (chat client as an MCP) -- an MCP is the natural home for a held socket that consumes pushes.
tasks.note: 2026-09-04: pr-master's coordination poller no longer touches the log. It now uses 'read --chan #ai-skills --since N' over the socket, which is a short-lived connection -- so it holds no subscriber (safe even before B122) and reads no file. Tschallacka pointed out that --since was the right tool all along; it had been ruled out by over-generalising from one wedged-server observation where both send and read failed, and never retested once the server was healthy. This closes the log-interfacing half of the violation for pr-master. What remains is the poll itself, which is T91a's push subscription.

tasks.title: chat-client-rs consumes broadcast PRIVMSG as it arrives, instead of looping on FETCH
tasks.detail: tail is currently a FETCH poll loop (src/chat-client-rs/src/main.rs around line 1594) and PRIVMSG is only inspected to confirm a send echoed (line 1041). Make the client a real subscriber: after backfilling from its cursor, follow the pushed stream and surface each message on arrival. Keep the cursor updated from pushed ids so a reconnect backfills correctly. Prove it with a test that a message reaches an attached client without any FETCH being issued after the join.

tasks.title: Turn ci-failures.sh into a pipeline-failure-retrieval skill, with glab alongside gh
tasks.detail:
ci-failures.sh landed as a maintainer script: given a run id, a PR number, a branch, or nothing (the current branch), it prints each failing job with the lines that identify the failure, and --raw keeps whole logs. It replaced a six-step hand dance that was performed eight times in one session.

It should become a skill, because the knowledge in it is not specific to this repository: which API answers while a run is still going, that the logs endpoint refuses a body without --allow-escape-sequences, that the colour codes then need stripping with a literal ESC because the escape form is a GNU extension, and which lines in a log actually identify a failure as opposed to merely mentioning one.

Add glab support beside gh, so the same command answers for a project hosted on either forge. The shapes differ and both need naming: gh has runs containing jobs, glab has pipelines containing jobs with a trace endpoint rather than a logs endpoint, and the failure vocabulary in a trace is not the same. The skill should detect which tool the remote calls for rather than being told, and say which it chose.

Worth carrying over from the script: resolving a bare number is ambiguous between a run id and a PR number, and it is disambiguated by magnitude, which is a heuristic that must be stated rather than hidden -- pr/47 is the unambiguous spelling. Also the extractor's own failure mode, found by pointing it at a ratchet failure it could not explain: 'FAIL (exit 1)' has a space before the paren, so a FAIL[:(] pattern missed the whole class, and continuing on indentation rather than a fixed line count is what keeps the next PASS row out of the extract.

Requested by Tschallacka on 2026-09-04, immediately after watching the manual version repeated once too often.

tasks.title: the chat MCP wakes on declared trigger phrases, not only on a nick mention
tasks.detail:
Michael: 'The mcp should have something baked in, that it actively triggers a wake on made trigger sentences.'

Today an agent wakes only when its nick appears. That misses the case that has cost the most here: an instruction addressed to nobody in particular. Measured twice in one session -- Michael wrote 'q6 write all configs, cleanup too' with no mention and it reached no agent, and B254 meant it could never be read afterwards either.

SHAPE. The adapter's wait tool takes a set of trigger phrases alongside the nick, declared once when the session registers rather than passed per call, and returns when any of them appears. The nick stays a trigger; it stops being the only one.

Points that decide the design, from what the shell version got wrong:
- Match the message TEXT, not the whole stored line. A stored line begins with its sender, so a naive pattern matches what an agent SAID and wakes it on its own messages -- t90 found exactly that in the shell example.
- Substring, not regex, unless a caller asks for a regex: a phrase is what a human types, and a regex metacharacter in it is a surprise.
- Case-insensitive by default for phrases, since an instruction is prose.
- The set belongs to the agent, not the channel: a nitpicker wants 'style' and 'comment', an installer agent wants 'install' and 'registration'.

The shell client should grow the same thing so the two front ends do not disagree, but the MCP is where it belongs first: it already holds a live connection, so it can match on arrival rather than polling a log.

Depends on nothing; B254 makes it more valuable but does not block it.
tasks.note:
SENDER-SCOPED TRIGGERS, Michael: 'triggers should be able to be sender specific, like if sender X sends FOO, then trigger.'

So a trigger is a pair, not a phrase: an optional sender and a phrase, either of which may be the wildcard.

- (sender, phrase) -- wake when X says FOO. The case Michael named.
- (any, phrase)     -- the plain phrase trigger.
- (sender, any)     -- wake on anything X says at all. This is the one that would have caught what was missed today: Michael wrote an instruction with no mention and no keyword, and no agent woke. An agent that trusts a particular sender should be able to say so once rather than guess at the words.
- (any, any) is the whole channel and is not a trigger; that is what read is for.

Why the sender half is not a nicety: a phrase alone fires on anyone repeating it, including an agent quoting the instruction back in the channel -- which is how a phrase trigger becomes a self-wake loop between two agents discussing the trigger. Scoping to a sender removes that.

Matching the sender: the stored line begins with the IRC prefix, so the sender is available without parsing the text. Compare against the NICK, not the prefix, and treat the suffixed form as the same sender until B283 is fixed -- while that stands, one agent posts as both name and name-2, and a sender-scoped trigger that only knows the plain nick silently stops firing the moment the peer reconnects.

tasks.title: install.sh needs a dev mode that installs the dev build dir, not the day-old shipped binaries
tasks.detail: Tschallacka: 'maybe add a dev mode, that respects the dev build dir, I think it didn't get updated.' He was right. There are two binary locations and the installer knows only one. setup-dev-env.sh builds this host's crates into the repo-root bin/<triple>/, which is where the skills look at runtime in a dev tree. install.sh copies from <skill>/bin/<triple>/, which only CI and a release populate. So running ./install.sh inside the repo -- which does NOT download, because download_source prefers a local tree when the script sits beside planning/SKILL.md -- silently installs whatever those shipped directories happen to hold. On 2026-09-08 that was a day-old ai-text-editor: the install downgraded a working editor to a build that predates expected_text on replace, mid-session, and the only symptom was a guard quietly no longer being accepted.\n\nWanted: a --dev flag (and a matching line in the summary saying which source each binary came from) that prefers bin/<triple>/<binary> over <skill>/bin/<triple>/<binary> when installing from a local tree, and refuses rather than silently skipping when neither exists. The summary must name the source, because 'installed' meaning two different things depending on an invisible directory is what made this cost an hour. Pairs with B291 (interactive-shell has no dev build at all) and B292 (cp cannot replace a running binary).
tasks.note: Also worth deciding whether setup-dev-env should populate <skill>/bin/<triple>/ directly instead, which would make one location serve both paths. That is the smaller change but it blurs 'shipped artifact' and 'local build', which is the distinction the release gates rely on. Reproduced concretely 2026-09-09: the day-old shipped binaries problem is not just stale content, it silently breaks the MCP protocol. ai-text-editor-mcp built 2026-09-04 vs source at 2026-09-07 advertised every tool with inputSchema {"additionalProperties":true,"type":"object"} (no properties, no required) -- 3 days of schema evolution (tab_id/tab_path/verbosity/expected_revision as named properties) missing entirely. Every mutating call (insert/replace/...) failed with revision_required no matter what was passed, with no indication the binary was stale -- the servers own staleness_notice/adapter_replaced() mechanism only fires on an in-session replacement, not on an adapter that was ALREADY stale when the session started. Confirms this needs either: install.sh dev mode using the freshly-built tree directly (this TODOs ask), or the MCP adapter checking its own build timestamp against the source it was compiled from and refusing/warning at initialize.

tasks.title: An update should detect the installed integration mode and keep it, not default back to skill
tasks.detail:
Updating a skill that has an integration mode must not need a flag to say which mode it is already in. Today it does, and the failure is silent in the dangerous direction: integration_mode_for (installer/src/05-config.sh) falls back to INTEGRATION_DEFAULT, which is 'skill', so a plain 'install.sh --all' over an mcp install reads as a request to switch to skill mode. remove_stale_integration_binaries then deletes the bridge binary and the MCP registration is torn down, on an update whose author only meant 'give me the newest version'.

Wanted precedence: an explicit --integration flag first, then the mode already installed, then INTEGRATION_DEFAULT for a first install. Two signals can establish the installed mode, and they should agree: integration.tsv maps mode to binary, so whichever declared binary is present in the destination's bin/<triple>/ names the mode; and the agent's own config carries the MCP registration for the mcp arm. Disagreement between them means a half-finished earlier switch, which is worth reporting rather than resolving silently.

The summary must say which mode was carried forward and where that was read from, because the whole point is that the caller no longer states it -- an install that silently picks a mode is what this task exists to remove, and replacing an explicit wrong default with an implicit one would not be progress. A first install of a skill with no prior state still needs the default, or a prompt when interactive.
tasks.note: Hit on 2026-09-08 installing master: both --integration ai-text-editor=mcp and --integration chat=skill had to be passed by hand, from knowledge of what was already there, purely to stop the update unregistering a running editor bridge. An updater that needs to be told the state it can see is a trap set for whoever forgets.

tasks.title: Select and shard the shell suite, so CI does not run 138 tests on 3 platforms for every commit
tasks.detail:
Two independent axes, and they compose. Numbers measured 2026-09-08: 138 shell tests, of which 116 (84%) are planning/tests, plus 86 crates.

SELECT. ci-scope.sh scopes CRATES only; the shell suite always runs in full. Extending the same idea to tests is the bigger win, and the pattern is already proven here. Shape: each test declares what it covers (a header marker), and a test whose covered paths do not intersect the change set is skipped. The invariant is the one ci-scope already states in its own docblock -- the default is always full, and every error path and every undeclared test runs. A selector that narrows when confused is worse than none, because the green tick then means 'we did not look' while reading as 'we looked'.

SHARD. Split what remains across runners with a deterministic --shard i/N over the sorted test list, matrixed in CI. It must be per-TEST, not per-suite: a suite-per-runner matrix would put 84% of the work on one leg. Deterministic assignment by sorted index keeps a test in the same shard so a CI failure is reproducible locally with the same flag. A required aggregate job depends on the shards so branch protection has one check to require.

Note the interaction with the machine-wide lock: shards are for CI, where each runner is its own machine. Locally the lock still serialises, which is correct -- see the one-verification-at-a-time hazard where a second concurrent run deletes the first's worktree.
tasks.note: Raised by Tschallacka: 'ci takes a long long time. and the more tests come, the longer it will take' and 'the entire suite tests everytime, even on binaries/paths that arent affected by the commit'. Sharding alone does not fix the second complaint; selection does. Sharding fixes the first and keeps fixing it as tests are added.

tasks.title: Ship a plugin that injects each subagent its own id at SubagentStart
tasks.detail:
Tschallacka asked whether a plugin could expose the per-subagent id. It can, and the whole chain was measured on 2026-09-08 rather than reasoned about.

WHAT WAS PROVEN, in order:

1. A SubagentStart hook exists and fires per subagent. It took effect immediately on being written to settings.json, with no session restart.

2. Its payload carries the identity nothing else does: agent_id, agent_type, plus session_id, prompt_id, cwd, scratchpad_dir and transcript_path. The agent_id matched, character for character, the id the Agent tool returned to the spawner -- a4631ac048e789cbb for the last probe.

3. hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext reaches the subagent's own context. A subagent asked to report its injected identity answered AGENT_ID=a4631ac048e789cbb TYPE=code-researcher having called no tools, so it read it from context rather than deriving it.

WHAT TO BUILD: a plugin shipping one SubagentStart hook that injects the agent's own id and type, and instructs it to pass that id as the session on every editor and chat call. The spawner needs to remember nothing and the subagent cannot be confused about who it is.

THE HONEST LIMIT: this is context injection, not an environment variable. The hook cannot set env for the subagent, because the subagent is not a new process -- so a CLI call from a subagent's bash still needs the id passed explicitly, and the subagent now knows it well enough to do that. Being context, it is also SOFT: the model has to use what it was told.

WHICH IS WHY IT PAIRS WITH THE REFUSAL. Soft supply plus a hard requirement is what makes it reliable: the hook guarantees every subagent HAS an id, and an editor that refuses an undeclared caller guarantees every subagent USES it. Neither half is sufficient alone -- injection without refusal is advisory, refusal without injection is an obstacle.
tasks.note:
DECIDED 2026-09-09, and these close the open design questions.

Q11a -- STRIP THE MODEL-FACING SESSION ARGUMENT from the MCP tool schemas. Once
the adapter can determine the caller itself, a session the model passes is
advisory at best; one that disagrees with the resolved identity is a mismatch to
refuse, not a value to trust.

Q12 -- GATE THE SKILL INSTALL PER HARNESS. A session-dependent tool installs as
an MCP on every harness, and as a skill only on codex and opencode, where a
plugin supplies the agent id for free. On Claude Code the identity would have to
come from the model on every call, which is a per-call token cost for something
the harness already knows, so the installer refuses the skill install there and
states the reason. Tschallacka's wording: the installer cannot offer the skill
install where the session cannot be guaranteed without extra token usage from the
agent on every single call.

STRUCTURE -- the resolution logic lives in the agent-session-key crate and is
called at the adapter's ENTRY POINT to record this run's session values, rather
than being scattered through the server. Where a harness supplies a per-call
identity that wins; the ladder is what runs when it does not; and where a harness
supplies none, mint an id and persist it for that worker.

MEASUREMENTS MOVED. The wire and hook findings for all three harnesses, both the
MCP side and the skill side, now live in .agents/knowledge/agent-identity-across-harnesses.md,
with the ladder and the procedure for adding an unmeasured harness in
src/agent-session-key/HARNESS-IDENTITY.md. Read those rather than this note; what
follows is only what they added on 2026-09-09.

CODEX, both surfaces. The MCP wire carries the identity outright:
params._meta["x-codex-turn-metadata"] holds session_id, thread_id, turn_id and
thread_source, where session_id is the CLI process and thread_id is the AGENT --
a subagent gets its own, matching SubagentStart's agent_id and the id the TUI
prints at spawn. No join needed. On the shell side codex DOES honour updatedInput,
contradicting the Claude Code result, but only alongside permissionDecision
"allow": without it the run fails with "PreToolUse hook returned updatedInput
without permissionDecision:allow". With both, a hook rewrote a command to carry
the agent id and the probe read it back.

OPENCODE, both surfaces. Its MCP wire carries nothing joinable -- only
progressToken -- and the plugin's callID never reaches the server, so the Claude
Code join is impossible there. Instead tool.execute.before can mutate output.args,
and shell.env merges into the command environment; both were measured giving a
parent and a subagent DISTINCT session ids while OPENCODE_PID was identical.

CLAUDE CODE, the shell side, which was the open half. A subagent's environment is
BYTE-IDENTICAL to its parent's: the only variable that differed was CLAUDE_EFFORT,
a model setting. CLAUDE_CODE_AGENT reads "claude" for a code-researcher subagent,
so it names the harness rather than the agent. With updatedInput refused for
command hooks, a Claude Code skill binary cannot learn who invoked it, and that is
what Q12 is decided on.

CORRECTION to the codex trust note recorded earlier: the trusted_hash covers the
hook REGISTRATION, not the script's contents. Rewriting the hook script at the
same path did not re-prompt, while adding a second registered event did. So a
trusted registration keeps trusting whatever that path later contains. Tool
approval is separate and per tool: the parent's "always allow" did not cover a
subagent's first call.

STILL OPEN: whether the individual binaries remain a shipped, agent-facing
surface. They are needed either way as the MCP server's substrate and by the test
suite; what Q12 decides is only whether they stay advertised, which is a
MODE/PACKAGE marker change rather than a code deletion.

tasks.title: The identity plugin installs with any session-dependent skill, as a hard requirement
tasks.detail:
Tschallacka's ruling: the SubagentStart identity plugin (T122) is not optional
where it is needed. A skill whose correctness depends on knowing WHICH agent is
calling must not install without it, because installing such a skill without it
produces the silent failure it exists to prevent -- two agents sharing one
session and neither able to tell.

WHICH SKILLS. The fact belongs to the skill rather than to a list in the
installer, matching how this repository registers everything else: the directory
is the registration. requires.tsv already declares "what this skill needs on the
target machine at runtime, and how badly", and a per-agent identity is exactly a
runtime need -- so it is a row there, and the existing unmet-requirement
machinery reports it. "MUST" is then expressible in the vocabulary already
present: the requirement is hard, not soft.

Session-dependent as measured today: chat (its session key decides the nick and
the per-channel cursors), ai-text-editor (session ownership of tabs, once T118
lands), interactive-shell (the session id names the socket). Confirm each
against its own code rather than inheriting this list.

THE STEP. Same shape as interactive_shell_permission_step and
editor_steering_step in installer/src/70-permissions.sh, which already know how
to touch settings.json safely: back the file up beside itself unless git tracks
it, read defensively with rjq, write through a mktemp and rename. It installs
the hook script into the agent root and registers the SubagentStart entry,
reports "already in place" on a second run rather than duplicating, and fires
only when a session-dependent skill is among those selected.

DECLINING IT MUST SAY WHAT IT COSTS, the way the editor steering warning does:
without the hook, every subagent shares its parent's session, so two agents will
write one cursor and hold one set of tabs, and neither will be told. That is a
silent wrong answer rather than a visible failure, which is the whole reason
this is a hard requirement.

NOT EVERY AGENT CAN HAVE IT. SubagentStart is Claude Code's hook. For an
opencode or codex root the step prints the manual equivalent and says plainly
that the guarantee is absent there, exactly as print_manual_interactive_shell_permissions
does -- rather than pretending the install is equivalent.

ORDER: T122 builds the plugin, this wires it into the installer. Doing this
first would register a hook that does not exist.
