tasks.title: What the resolver already does, so it is ported rather than redesigned
tasks.detail: planning/scripts/register-resolve.sh is working, mutation-tested and bash-3.2 clean; its test is planning/tests/test-register-resolve.sh (7 sections). Behaviour worth keeping verbatim: reads the three index stages rather than branch names, so it works mid-conflict with no checkout; --check exits 1 on a conflicted register and 0 on a clean one, for use in a pre-push or CI hook; lists each collision with BOTH sides' titles plus a suggested free id taken from the high-water mark of both sides; refuses when a decision is missing, naming which; reports what each side changed since the merge base, separating 'modified on one side ONLY - read these keys' from 'modified identically on both sides, so the base is simply older' so nothing is falsely suspected; refuses a divergence with an explanation of why renaming would not help; checks EACH SIDE for soundness before asking for decisions, so an already-unsound branch is reported as that branch's fault rather than blamed on the decisions; follows renames into parent and into blocked_on when its whole value is the id; REPORTS prose mentions and never rewrites them, because an id inside a sentence may be a prefix of a longer id or belong to the other register; prints the resolved register to stdout and the confirmation to stderr; writes nothing until CONFIRM=<hash> is handed back, and the hash is identical under bash 5.3 and 3.2. Verified against the real conflict in PR #13, where it correctly refused because that branch's own register is unsound (B105).

tasks.title: Packaging and registration rules a new shipped script must satisfy
tasks.detail: 1) Every file declares MODE: PROD (the user receives it) or MODE: DEV (only a maintainer does); an unmarked tracked file fails tests/test-mode-markers.sh. Syntax follows the format: '# MODE: X' in shell, '<!-- MODE: X -->' in Markdown, and AFTER any YAML frontmatter. No comment line may BEGIN with the marker keyword or the generators strip it. 2) install.sh is generated - never edit it; edit installer/src/NN-*.sh and run ./installer/build.sh, which the installer-build CI job verifies byte-for-byte. 3) A new file under planning/ needs PACKAGE-MANIFEST.tsv and PACKAGE-MAP.tsv rows too, compared byte-for-byte so ROW ORDER matters; a file under bug-report/ or todo/ needs only the skill_files() arm, because those two registries are planning-only. 4) package.json's files array ships whole skill directories, and npm's rule is that a path included that way CANNOT be excluded by .npmignore or .gitignore - that is how untracked local notes nearly got published (B100), and it is why a register inside a skill directory would ship (B107). 5) After adding a shipped file, planning/tests/fixtures/overview/npm-package-baseline.tsv must be regenerated: the test compares npm pack output against it byte-size by byte-size. 6) test-flag-coverage.sh requires every accepted flag to be documented in --help AND referenced by a test. 7) Both skills already declare rjq hard in requires.tsv, so a shipped helper may rely on it; nothing else may be added to that budget - python3 is banned outright, not even guarded.

tasks.title: How to verify this work, and what a green run does not prove
tasks.detail: Run in this order: bash -n on every edited script; shellcheck at the severity CI uses, which is --severity=warning and NOT --severity=error as AGENTS.md still says (T75) - and the five generated plan-*-lib.sh must be built and NAMED on the command line, because shellcheck resolves a source= directive only against files given to it, so omitting them reports every variable read from them as unassigned; then the targeted tests; then ./run-tests.sh (123 test files, about 6-7 minutes); then bash32-run-tests for the bash 3.2 floor, which matters because 'bash32 ./run-tests.sh' is NOT the same test - children resolve to whatever bash PATH offers, so the wrapper that prepends a 3.2 bin dir is the only honest form. Known-failing on a developer box and NOT caused by your change: test-runtime-dependencies (fails identically on unmodified master here, passes in CI) and test-npm-package (fails whenever the working tree has uncommitted shipped-file changes, and aborts early via npm pack's prepack hook when the per-target chat binaries are absent - build them with ./setup-dev-env.sh or the baseline comparison never runs at all). Mutation-test every assertion added: revert the fix, watch the test fail, restore. An assertion never seen to fail is not verified, and a passing test after a mutation that changed no file is not evidence.

tasks.title: Tools available for register work, and where they came from (PR #15)
tasks.detail: PR #15 adds two things any agent touching BUGS.json or TODO.json should know about. (1) planning/scripts/register-resolve.sh resolves an id collision in a conflicted register. Usage: '--check <register>' exits 1 when conflicted and 0 when clean, so it fits a hook; '<register>' with no decisions lists every collision with BOTH sides' titles plus a suggested free id and exits 65; '<register> side:old:new side:old:new ...' takes every decision in ONE run, applies them, and prints the resolved register to stdout with a confirmation on stderr; re-running the SAME command prefixed with CONFIRM=<that hash> writes it in place. side is ours|theirs or either branch name. It reads git index stages (:1 base, :2 ours, :3 theirs) so it needs no checkout, refuses a divergence (both sides editing one base entry differently) as something a rename cannot fix, refuses to resolve into a register whose own side is already unsound, follows a rename into parent and into an id-valued blocked_on, and REPORTS prose mentions rather than rewriting them. (2) tests/test-register-soundness.sh runs the rules over the committed registers, which nothing did before: a finding there means the entry did not come from the writers, because bug-add.sh and todo-update.sh refuse exactly those. Run it after any hand edit. Both are MODE: DEV and repository-side only - shipping equivalents to the two skills is T81.

tasks.title: Support Windows in interactive-shell
tasks.detail: interactive-shell is the workspace's first POSIX-only member and is excluded from the x86_64-pc-windows-msvc leg of the native CI job. The exclusion is correct for that target but it is not the end state: Michael wants Windows supported, including driving powershell.exe and cmd.exe. The unix socket is NOT what blocks it -- a loopback port would replace it, as the chat skill already offers. The terminal core is what blocks it: libc::openpty (lib.rs:1415), ioctl TIOCSCTTY (1437) and TIOCSWINSZ (1897), setsid (1436), setpgid (1443), and kill(-pid, SIGKILL/SIGTERM) (1463, 1473, 1482), plus twelve raw-fd sites against a platform whose equivalent is a HANDLE. The libc crate exposes none of openpty/setsid/TIOCSCTTY for windows targets -- twenty hits across its unix modules, zero in its windows module. Two independent routes, filed as sub-tasks: Cygwin's POSIX layer is cheap and yields a Cygwin bash; a native ConPTY backend is the real work and is the only route that drives PowerShell and cmd.

tasks.title: Add an x86_64-pc-cygwin leg so the POSIX code runs unchanged
tasks.detail: Cygwin implements ptys, sessions, process groups and signals, so the existing POSIX code needs little or no change - this is a toolchain excursion, not a port. Verified against the pinned toolchain: rustc 1.98 does list x86_64-pc-cygwin in rustc --print target-list, so the compiler knows it, but it is absent from rustup target list, which means tier 3 with no prebuilt std. It therefore needs nightly with -Z build-std or a hand-built std, which is why this is filed rather than done. Deliverables: the target building in CI as its own matrix leg, and a Windows row in interactive-shell/binaries.tsv so the shipped set matches what CI proves. What this does NOT deliver is PowerShell or cmd - a Cygwin build drives a Cygwin bash, and the native shells are T84b. MSYS is tracked separately as T84c because it is a different runtime DLL, not a variant of this one.

tasks.title: Add a native ConPTY backend so PowerShell and cmd can be driven
tasks.detail: What Michael actually asked for: interactive-shell driving powershell.exe and cmd.exe. That means a second terminal backend behind the same protocol, because Windows has no analogue of the calls the current one makes. CreatePseudoConsole/ResizePseudoConsole/ClosePseudoConsole replace openpty and the two ioctls; a Job Object with TerminateJobObject replaces setpgid plus kill(-pid, ...), since Windows has neither process groups nor POSIX signals; HANDLEs replace the raw fds; and the client transport moves to a loopback port, which is the one piece that ports without argument. Keep the wire protocol identical so the agent-facing surface does not fork per platform, and cfg-gate the backends rather than the crate -- an inert Windows stub that builds and refuses to run is worse than an honest absence. ConPTY needs Windows 10 1809 or newer. Michael wants BOTH routes, so this does not retire T84a: they cover different shells on the same platform, and the two backends can share the protocol and the tests.

tasks.title: Target MSYS2 as well, which has no upstream rust target
tasks.detail: Michael wants MSYS2 targeted alongside Cygwin, and it is not the same build. msys2-runtime is a fork of the Cygwin runtime with the same POSIX surface, so the interactive-shell code should need no change, but a binary for it links msys-2.0.dll where a Cygwin binary links cygwin1.dll, and the two are not interchangeable at runtime. The obstacle is sharper than T84a: rustc --print target-list on the pinned 1.98 toolchain lists x86_64-pc-cygwin and NO msys target whatsoever, so unlike Cygwin there is not even a tier-3 target to build std for. The likely route is a custom target spec derived from the cygwin one with the runtime library swapped, built under MSYS2 own toolchain - to be established rather than assumed, so treat the first step as research and record what is found here before writing CI. This is also the Git-for-Windows route in practice: Git for Windows ships the MSYS2 runtime, so whatever makes MSYS2 work is what makes a Git-for-Windows bash work. Its source is public at git-for-windows/git and git-for-windows/msys2-runtime; nothing needs vendoring here to settle the approach.

tasks.title: a question skill: numbered questions with lettered options, never an unordered list
tasks.detail: Questions put to the human carry an increasing numeric id within the session -- Q1, Q2, Q3 -- and never restart at 1 for a new batch, so an answer of 'Q1' is unambiguous. One question per number. A multipart question is sub-numbered (Q20a, Q20b), never bulleted. When a question offers options or suggested answers they are lettered a, b, c, d, e, so the human can answer 'Q7b' rather than quoting text back. There is ALWAYS a final letter meaning 'none of these, I will say it myself' -- a closed set of options is a leading question. Never an unordered list for either the questions or the options: a bullet cannot be referenced, so an answer covering three of four parts leaves no way to say which one was missed. Repeat the number when following up, say which number an answer resolved, and carry an unanswered number forward unrenumbered rather than dropping it. Requested by Tschallacka on 2026-09-04; the same rules are already in his global CLAUDE.md, and this task is to make them a shipped skill so every agent follows them, not only this one.

tasks.title: retire read/tail --local, the log-file path that bypasses the server
tasks.detail: read --local and tail --local walk $AI_CHAT_HOME/channels/<chan>.log with no server. Remove them, or keep them only as a maintenance escape hatch that is documented as such and never recommended in an agent instruction or skill doc. Sweep SKILL.md, the client's own usage text and .agents docs for anywhere --local is offered as the way to read a channel, since that is what teaches every future agent to bypass the socket. Depends on T91a: nothing may lose the ability to read a channel before the push path replaces it.

tasks.title: make the server's fan-out structurally lock-safe: a real channel per peer, and a read-write registry
tasks.detail:
PR #43 fixed the acute wedge by giving each connection an outbox that its own thread drains, so a broadcaster never writes another peer's socket. That is the right shape, hand-rolled. Finish it properly:

(1) The outbox is a Mutex<Vec<String>> plus drain. The idiomatic form is one std::sync::mpsc::Sender per connection: the message is MOVED to the owner, the channel's lock is a true leaf that is never held across I/O, and no code can accidentally reach a peer's connection state again. A hand-rolled queue invites someone to add 'just one' extra field guarded by the same mutex.

(2) The registry is 'writers: Mutex<Vec<Arc<Mutex<Option<ConnState>>>>>' -- a mutex holding a vector of mutexes. It is READ on every broadcast and WRITTEN only on connect and disconnect, so it wants an RwLock. This matters beyond speed: the accept loop needs that same lock to register an arrival, which is why a stalled broadcast stopped new clients being served at all.

(3) While in there, the connection state's own mutex is held across a 200ms read and immediately retaken, which is what starved broadcasters (measured by chat-b122). Whatever survives after (1), that pattern should not.

CONSIDERED AND REJECTED, recorded so it is not re-proposed: dropping server-side fan-out entirely and letting our clients read the log, or poll FETCH, because they largely do that already. Tschallacka's rule on 2026-09-04 forecloses it -- nothing outside the server may touch the log, and steady-state delivery is a push over the socket, not a poll. Fan-out is therefore load-bearing and gets fixed, not deleted. See T91a.

Not urgent: the acute bug is fixed. This is the cleanup that stops it recurring by construction rather than by care.

tasks.title: CI merges the registers branch to master on push, and refuses anything but the registers in it
tasks.detail:
Half of the register policy is in place: pre-push-check refuses a BUGS.json or TODO.json change on any branch but 'registers', names that branch in the refusal, and AGENTS.md documents why. The other half -- Tschallacka's original design -- is not built: 'bugs branch gets merged automatically by ci on push, only bugs.json and todo.json may be modified in that ci'.

What is missing:

1. A workflow on push to 'registers' that validates and fast-forwards master. Validation is cheap and already exists: 'bugs check' and reg_findings decide soundness, and a duplicate-id scan is the one thing git cannot see -- two branches taking the same next free id merge textually with NO conflict, which is how eight duplicate ids landed on 2026-09-04.

2. That workflow must REFUSE a push to 'registers' touching anything except BUGS.json and TODO.json. Without it the branch becomes a protection bypass: register changes skip review by design, so anything else riding along would too.

3. Master is protected and requires a successful CI run, so the workflow needs a way to land the merge -- a token with permission, or the branch protection amended for this one path. That decision is Tschallacka's, not a worker's, because it widens who can write master.

Until it exists, a registers push is an ordinary PR against master, which is what today's entries did (B162-B164, T92). That works but leaves the register waiting on a human, which is the friction the design was meant to remove.

Raised from the transition itself: the rule shipped naming a branch ('bugs') that git cannot create while any bugs/* ref exists, so it had to be renamed to 'registers' in PR #48 before a single entry could be filed under it.

tasks.title: Interactive installer TUI has no way to choose a skill's integration mode (mcp vs skill)
tasks.detail: install.sh's --integration flag lets an automation caller pick ai-text-editor's mcp bridge vs its skill client, but the interactive terminal UI (iui_info_actions and the rest of the iui_ pane rendering) only offers 'install dependencies' / 'reverify dependencies' as actions -- there is no toggle or prompt anywhere in the TUI for integration mode. A human running the plain interactive installer cannot choose mcp mode at all; only a scripted --integration flag can. Add an action (or a per-skill toggle in the info pane) that lets an interactive user pick among the modes integration_modes() declares for the skill under the cursor, for skills that offer more than one.
tasks.note: Implemented on fix/worktrees-tmpdir-chat-relay at eb076758; closes on merge. The info pane gains an m action for a skill declaring more than one mode, naming the mode in force and cycling it. Two things the implementation had to move: integration_mode_for() to 05-config.sh (install-ui.sh does not source 50-manifest.sh, so a ui function calling it would repeat B49), and the generated INTEGRATION block into iui_dev_load_tables (the mode tables live only in the artifact, so the standalone picker had an empty integration_modes and would have rendered no line).

tasks.title: jump points: on open, derive a file's outbound references from CodeGraph so a tab can be navigated, not just searched
tasks.detail: SKIP
tasks.note:
LIFECYCLE settled with Michael: derive the jump points at open, and RECOMPUTE THEM ON SAVE. Save is the right boundary because codegraph indexes DISK -- save is the moment disk changes -- so staleness is bounded to 'while the tab is dirty' rather than being open-ended. A set still carries the revision it was computed at, so a dirty tab's jump points are reported stale rather than followed silently.

COST: all of this is server-side, so the scanning, caching and re-derivation cost the agent NO TOKENS. The agent pays only for the jump points it asks for. That is what justifies doing the work eagerly at open and at every save, rather than lazily on request.

INDEX FRESHNESS, worth handling explicitly: codegraph's watcher lags a write by about a second, so a recompute fired immediately on save can read the pre-save index. Run 'codegraph sync' first -- it is incremental and prints 'Already up to date' when there is nothing to do, so a needless run is free -- then re-derive. Useful side effect: editing through the editor would keep the codegraph index warm, which the repository already asks callers to do by hand after changing code.

tasks.title: split chat-client-rs/src/lib.rs into modules
tasks.detail: lib.rs is 2776 lines: the CLI entry point, the CLI verbs, the resolution ladder, the TLS connect and TOFU pin, the session, the local log reader and an in-file test module, in one file. It reached that size as one file because it was main.rs; T90 made it a library without splitting it, deliberately, so an in-flight B266 change on another branch would merge as a rename rather than fight a mass code move. Once feat/t90-chat-mcp and fix/worktrees-tmpdir-chat-relay are both merged that reason is spent. Split by concern, one docblock each: net (resolve, connect, client_config, the TOFU pin, line I/O, wait_for_welcome), discovery (the beacon, the cache, resolve_server), session (the key ladder, Session, cursors), wire (wire_segments, split_at_budget, msg_line_id), local (the channel log reader), and the CLI verbs behind run(). The public surface is already the split: what the MCP adapter imports is exactly the first four groups.

tasks.title: installable agent profiles: ship .agents/profiles/ the way skills are shipped
tasks.detail:
The nitpicker profile lives at .agents/profiles/nitpicker.md and is installed by hand: copy it to ~/.claude/agents/ and restart the session. Nothing declares it, nothing installs it, and nothing checks the copy has not drifted from the repository's.

Skills already solve this: a manifest declares the files, install.sh writes them into each agent root, and a test refuses a tracked file nobody declared. Profiles need the same treatment, with two differences that decide the shape:

- The destination differs per harness. Claude Code reads ~/.claude/agents/, and codex and opencode place agent definitions elsewhere; the installer already resolves per-agent roots for skills, so this is the same resolution, not a new one.
- A profile is only picked up at session start. The registry is read once, so an install has to say plainly that a restart is required before the profile can be used, the way the skill install already tells the reader to restart the agent CLI.

Consumers: installer/src/50-manifest.sh (skill_files or a profiles equivalent), PACKAGE-MANIFEST.tsv and PACKAGE-MAP.tsv, installer/build.sh, and a declarations test so a new profile cannot be added without being declared.

Filed at Michael's request while adding the first profile to the repository.

tasks.title: The session owner needs a Windows transport: loopback TCP with a token
tasks.detail:
T107 landed the owner on unix sockets. Windows has no unix socket, so control.rs carries a cfg(not(unix)) arm where serve() and ask() both return None -- every verb there keeps exactly the behaviour it had before T107, including the B283 suffix when a tail is running.

The shape it needs is the one ai-text-editor already uses: bind loopback TCP on an ephemeral port, put the port and a secret in the owner record, and prove the secret per connection rather than sending it in the request. The record already carries pid and started_at_ns for owner identity; what it gains is the endpoint form and the token. src/ai-text-editor/src/transport.rs is the reference, including why the token is not in the envelope.

Two things must hold that the unix path gets for free: the record file's permissions are the only guard on a loopback port (there is no 0700 directory doing it), and liveness is still decided by connecting, not by the pid. A port that nothing answers is a stale record, same as a socket that refuses.

Not shipped with T107 deliberately: an untested socket transport on a platform nobody here can run is worse than an honest fallback, and the fallback is correct -- just without the fix.
tasks.note: chat/binaries.tsv does ship chat-client-rs.exe for x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, so this is a real supported target and not a hypothetical one.

tasks.title: Relocating a block should not cost its content: a move (and copy) verb
tasks.detail:
Today the only way to relocate text is to write it at the destination and delete it at the source, so the block's full content is generated as an argument even though the server already holds it. On a large document a refactor is mostly REARRANGEMENT, which means paying output tokens for content that never changed.

Proposed: move --from-range-start/--from-range-end (or a span token, see T110) plus a destination, resolved and applied server-side with no content in the request. copy the same without the delete. Both are guarded the way replace is -- the source span is verified before anything is removed -- and both report what they moved, so the caller can verify from the answer as it can today.

Why it is worth its own entry rather than folding into T110: T110 removes the GUARD's cost, this removes the CONTENT's cost, and they are independent. A move with no guard is still a move; a guarded replace still pays for its text.

Undo already file-backs large edits, so the snapshot machinery a move needs exists. The ordering question to settle: a move within one tab is one atomic operation, not an insert plus a delete that could half-apply -- begin_transaction/end_transaction is the existing shape to reuse or to say why it is not enough.
tasks.note: Raised by Tschallacka asking whether the pasted content can be limited to buy back context: 'on a large document with a lot of edits that would suck badly.' Measured in this session: guards were mostly 1-4 lines, but one replacement was 185 lines, so the replacement is the dominant cost and a rearrangement pays it for nothing.

tasks.title: Abbreviate tab ids to the shortest unambiguous prefix, git-style
tasks.detail:
A tab id is a 64-character hex uuid and it is repeated in every response. Measured 2026-09-08 on a two-line read at verbosity 0: the payload is 121 bytes and 76 of them -- 62 percent -- are the tab id. The file content being read was 32 bytes.

Tschallackas design: return the shortest prefix that is unambiguous among the live tabs, and let it grow as tabs are added. One tab starting cd0 with nothing else starting c is returned as c; open a second c tab and both lengthen to the first distinguishing character.

Where it goes. session::resolve_tab already reads every record and already filters by tab_uuid equality, so it is the natural home: match by PREFIX instead, group the matches by tab_uuid first, and refuse when two DISTINCT uuids share the prefix -- naming the candidates, which is the doctrine the rest of that module already follows for stale or ambiguous identities. Several records for ONE uuid stay as they are, newest-by-start_time wins. A full 64-character id must keep resolving exactly as today, so nothing that stored one breaks.

The emitting side is the other half: whatever writes tab_id into a response (T98 put it on every response at every verbosity) has to write the abbreviated form.

The one honest hazard, which git has too: a short id an agent is holding can become ambiguous when a new tab opens. That is recoverable and must be made so -- the refusal names the candidates, and the agent re-resolves. It must never silently pick one.
tasks.note:
Raised by Tschallacka on seeing a verbosity-0 response: 'why are the tab ids so large'. A 2-character id takes that same wire frame from 303 to 241 bytes, and the payload from 121 to 58. RE-KEYING IS AN EVENT, NOT A FIELD (Tschallacka). If ids are not echoed on every response (T119), then the only moment a caller needs to be told an id is when it CHANGED -- a new tab opened, the shortest unambiguous prefix grew, and the handle the caller is holding is now too short. The server says that ONCE, naming which tabs were re-keyed and to what, rather than paying for the id on every answer against the chance it moved.

That also disposes of the ambiguity hazard this entry worried about. A held short id does not silently rot: the caller is told at the moment it stopped being unique, so a refusal for ambiguity becomes the fallback rather than the mechanism. Q9 RULED (Tschallacka): the Worktree rung is not trusted to OWN tabs. Identity
comes from the plugin, and where no plugin can supply one -- codex, opencode,
a bare CLI -- the client mints its own and persists it for that worker, so the
behaviour is the same everywhere rather than degrading on the agents that
cannot be told who they are.

So the ladder splits by purpose, which it never did before. Worktree stays a
fine way to FIND a live server; it stops being a way to SAY WHO YOU ARE. Only
a declared or minted id owns tabs.

The carrier already exists and does not need inventing: the editor has
--save-session-token PATH to write one and --session-token PATH to reuse it,
which is mint-and-persist under another name. Minting an id and saving it
through that path gives the second call the identity the first one created.

THE LIMIT, which must be stated rather than discovered later. Persistence needs
somewhere to persist TO, and for a worker made of many short-lived CLI
processes the only anchors available are the filesystem and the environment.
Both are per-LOCATION, not per-worker. So a minted id is stable and exclusive
against everything except a second worker starting in the same place with the
same anchor, which is exactly the collision the Worktree rung had. Minting does
not remove that case; it narrows it to agents that have no plugin AND share a
location AND run at once.

That residue is acceptable on its own terms, and worth naming for what it is: on
Claude Code the hook removes it entirely, because every subagent arrives with an
explicit id whatever its worktree. Elsewhere it is a smaller version of the
problem rather than a solved one, and an agent in that position can always pass
--session and be certain.

WHAT MINTING MUST NOT DO: silently mint a fresh id per invocation. That never
collides and is therefore tempting, but it loses every tab between calls, so the
session it names is empty each time. Persisting is the whole substance of the
ruling; the minting is the easy half.


WHY THE ALTERNATIVES ARE OUT, in Tschallackas words: they are "too iffy and conflict hungry". That is the operative objection rather than mere imprecision -- an identity derived from a worktree, a pid or a harness variable does not simply identify less well, it actively puts two workers on one identity and neither is told. A minted id is exclusive by construction, which is the property being bought.

tasks.title: Make a mangled shell argument suggest the editor, the way in-place writes already do
tasks.detail:
Tschallacka's idea: backticks and command substitution inside a prose-bearing
shell argument should trigger the same nudge the editor gate already gives for
in-place stream editing and heredocs.

The gate already owns exactly this judgement. It intercepts a Bash command,
decides the shell is the wrong tool for it, and names the right one. What it
watches for today is writing to a path. What it does not watch for is prose
being passed THROUGH a shell, which fails differently: not refused, not
errored, just quietly altered.

Detect a quoted argument carrying a backtick or a dollar-paren where the
command is a register writer, and answer the way the gate already answers:
say what will happen to the text, and name the editor plus a file as the route
that cannot damage it. That route needs T120's file input to exist first, or
the nudge points nowhere.

Worth a rule of its own because the failure is SILENT. A refused command
teaches immediately; a command that succeeds with a word missing teaches
nothing, and the entry it wrote looks complete.

Evidence for the whole idea, from filing this very entry: the first attempt was
REFUSED by the gate because the detail text mentioned the in-place editor by
name in prose. So the gate already reads argument text -- it simply reads it
for the wrong thing, matching a tool name where it should be matching a
substitution that will alter the argument. The two changes belong together:
stop firing on prose that merely names a tool, start firing on prose that the
shell is about to rewrite.
tasks.note: The hook lives outside this repository, in the user hooks directory, so this entry is the design and the argument rather than the patch. Pairs with T120: the nudge is only honest once there is somewhere to nudge towards. Also strengthens the prose false positive already reported under B297.

tasks.title: ai-text-editor MCP: accept 'path' as an alias for 'file' on every tool that takes it
tasks.detail: Every tool's real parameter is 'file' (open, insert, replace, ...), but 'path' is the far more natural/common name an agent reaches for -- it is what open() and most file APIs call it, and it is what this session actually typed on the first two open calls today. Since the schema has additionalProperties: false, a caller who says 'path' gets no error and no file at all: the request silently proceeds with file=None, falls through to identity-based resolution, and can surface an unrelated, confusing failure (in this case session_stale, which had nothing to do with the real mistake). Wanted: accept 'path' as a synonym for 'file' in the MCP adapter's payload parsing (src/ai-text-editor-mcp/src/lib.rs's call_tool, where 'file' is read out of the arguments object), and/or have request construction refuse an unrecognized top-level key near 'file' rather than silently proceeding with none. Consider whether the tool schema's 'file' description should also say '(aka path)' so this is documented at the point of use.

tasks.title: interactive-shell: a hook that recommends the skill when an agent says a command needs a tty/interactive input
tasks.detail: An agent that tries a headless command, hits a tty/stdin requirement, and then tells the user something like 'I can't do this because it needs interactive input/a terminal/a tty' has just described exactly the situation this skill exists for -- but nothing points it there in the moment. Wanted: a hook (Stop is the natural candidate, since it can see the assistant's own just-produced text; PostToolUse on Bash could instead pattern-match the COMMAND's own stderr for tty/stdin refusals, which is a stronger, less false-positive-prone signal but only catches the raw error, not an agent explaining it in an already-decided response) that recognizes this admission-of-defeat pattern (mentions of tty, interactive, 'requires input', 'not a terminal', stdin-is-not-a-tty style phrasing, arriving after a Bash tool call) and injects a reminder naming interactive-shell as the way to actually drive the program. The two candidate hook points have different tradeoffs -- worth deciding which (or both) before building: a Bash-output pattern match is more reliable but can only fire once, at the tool-result boundary already past the assistant's own words, while a Stop-hook text scan can catch the assistant's own summary/refusal even when the underlying error was noisier or spread across several attempts. False positives (a command that fails for an unrelated reason while incidentally mentioning 'terminal', e.g. a terminal-emulator config error) need a plan too.

tasks.title: interactive-shell: a hook that reminds the skill exists BEFORE an agent works around a TTY requirement, not only after it admits defeat
tasks.detail: T125 covers the 'admission of defeat' pattern: an agent tries a headless command, hits a tty/stdin error, and tells the user it can't do this. There is a distinct, earlier pattern T125's hook never sees: an agent that notices a program needs a TTY and proactively reasons its way AROUND that, choosing a workaround instead of ever attempting the interactive path -- e.g. Michael's example: 'msync needs a TTY for its source chooser. It has an --environment flag though -- trying that first, since a non-interactive path beats a PTY.' No error occurs, no refusal is stated, so T125's tty/stdin-refusal pattern match and its PostToolUse-on-Bash-stderr variant both never fire; the workaround is chosen silently in the agent's own reasoning before any command even runs. This is worth its own entry because the fix is different in kind: T125's hook watches an OUTCOME (a failed command, an admission), while this one would need to watch a DECISION being made in the assistant's own text -- closer to a Stop-hook or UserPromptSubmit-hook scan for phrasing like 'needs a TTY/terminal/interactive input' followed by 'instead' or 'so I will use X', regardless of whether anything was ever run. False positives need the same care T125 already flags (a program that merely mentions a terminal for unrelated reasons).
tasks.note: Reported by Michael, relayed via bridge:session_0114UV8CPfYa9xkB93JbKSDx (relay-ai-skills) after searching TODO.json and interactive-shell/SKILL.md and finding no existing match for the trigger sentence.

tasks.title: ai-text-editor MCP: codex prompts for permission on every call, and the resulting delay routinely expires the servers idle timeout mid-task
tasks.detail: Michael, driving ai-text-editor via codex: codex asks for approval on every single ai-text-editor.open/read/search call, unlike a normal read-only tool. Each approval adds real wall-clock delay between calls, and the autostarted ai-text-editor-server has its own idle_timeout_seconds (open calls in the transcript pass 120, then 300). When the approval delay across several calls exceeds that window, the server exits and every open tab_id in flight goes tab_unknown - "no session record has tab_id X; the tab may belong to a server that has since exited - open the file again for a current id (the journal replays)". Codex then has to reopen the same file and retry, compounding the prompt fatigue. Two angles worth investigating together, since fixing either alone only helps half the symptom: (1) why codex prompts per-call at all for a local read-only-by-default MCP server - check whether ai-text-editor tools/list declares read-only tool annotations (e.g. an MCP readOnlyHint-style hint) that a conforming client could use to skip confirmation, and what codexs own MCP trust/allowlist config supports; (2) whether the servers idle_timeout_seconds should scale with, or be immune to, the callers own confirmation latency - a tab dying because a HUMAN was slow to click approve is a different failure than a tab dying because the agent went idle, and only the second is what the timeout is meant to catch.
tasks.note: Reported by Michael 2026-09-09, relayed via bridge:session_0114UV8CPfYa9xkB93JbKSDx (relay-ai-skills) from a codex transcript driving ai-text-editor directly - real tab_unknown errors and re-opens shown in the transcript, not hypothesized.

tasks.title: explorative: a JSONL session-transcript pruner that shrinks provably-static/superseded content in place
tasks.detail:
Validated end to end today (relay session, not yet a shipped tool): took a real subagent transcript (129 lines, 639KB) that wrote a short story via ai-text-editor one-paragraph-per-call, then revised it twice (rain->hail/mountainous, then farmer->farmers wife) via search/replace. Wrote a pruning script that NEVER deletes a line and NEVER touches uuid/parentUuid/type or any structural key - it only replaces the heavy VALUE of specific known-safe fields with a short placeholder, in place. Targeted: (1) attachment entries of type skill_listing/prompt_snapshot - static, harness-regenerated on resume; (2) an inlined SKILL.md from a Skill-tool invocation - re-readable from disk; (3) ai-text-editor search tool_results that are provably superseded the instant their matching replace lands. Result: 129 lines unchanged, 9 lines content-shrunk, 639KB->438KB (31.5%). Verified structural integrity (identical line count, identical uuid/parentUuid/type/key-set on every line) then did the real test: swapped the pruned file in for the LIVE subagent transcript, resumed the subagent, and gave it a 9-part questionnaire about all three story states from memory (not by re-reading the file). It answered every question correctly, including a specific self-correction detail only recoverable from genuine memory, then performed a normal ai-text-editor read afterward with no corruption (correct revision, dirty:false, disk_diverged:false).

FURTHER OPTIMIZATION, Michaels idea, also confirmed against real data today: when a replace call is guarded by expected_text (or when a search precedes a replace with the same literal text), the OLD text ends up duplicated up to three times in one edits transcript lines - the search --query argument itself, an echoed "SEARCH '<query>' -> byte_start=X byte_end=Y" line some callers print, and the replace responses own deleted.text field. The replace responses deleted.text is authoritative (server-confirmed exact text actually removed), so the other two occurrences of the same string are redundant once the replace response exists. Proposed shrink: for a search --query argument or an echoed SEARCH line whose text is later confirmed verbatim in a subsequent replace responses deleted.text/expected_text, replace it with a short stub - first 7 words ... last 7 words - since the replace response already carries the authoritative full text, and the write it produced is what is recorded anyway.

WHAT NEEDS BUILDING (exploratory, not a fixed spec): a general tool (script or hook) that (a) walks a session or subagent JSONL transcript, (b) identifies the same category of provably-static or provably-superseded content by structural pattern rather than by hardcoded byte offsets, (c) applies the search/replace-text-deduplication shrink above, (d) never deletes a line or touches structural keys, (e) is conservative by construction - skip anything it cannot positively classify as safe, since format details WILL drift and a false-positive prune (deleting something still load-bearing) is much worse than a missed one. Motivation: an ai-text-editor MCP audit this session found ai-text-editor tool results accounting for 28 percent of one sessions context-cache usage, traced to one long-running, never-compacted session (990 calls over 3 days); this pruning technique is a complementary lever to auto-compact tuning, operating on transcripts directly rather than only at compaction time.

If the JSONL/session-transcript format changes in the future, adapt the classifier rather than assuming the shapes documented here are permanent - they were reverse-engineered empirically, not from documentation.
tasks.note: Requested by Michael 2026-09-09, explorative work done in the ai-skills-relay session (bridge:session_0114UV8CPfYa9xkB93JbKSDx). The 129-line test transcript and prune.py script that produced these numbers live at ~/git/tester/transcript-experiment/ on Tschallackas machine - not committed anywhere, throwaway experiment artifacts, ask him for a copy if useful as a starting point rather than rebuilding from scratch.

tasks.title: A postmortem template carrying token accounting and a reviewer-session table
tasks.detail: The unbuilt half of T58, separated rather than folded into its close. codex's postmortem recommendation 10, and the artifact that made their run legible in the first place: seventeen cycles, 109 findings and 41.7 million tokens, with a per-cycle table of session id, elapsed time and findings count. That data existed only because they went and collected it by hand afterwards. T57 now seeds the per-cycle fields in the review-scope block, so a template would have something to read rather than asking someone to reconstruct it. It has no natural home in the plan documents — a postmortem is written after the plan is finished and describes the process rather than the work — so it needs a decision about where it lives before it is written.

tasks.title: Address an edit by anchor or symbol, so an endpoint is never inferred
tasks.detail:
A replace is addressed by two integers today. The start usually comes from a search and is sound; the END is often inferred -- 'up to where the next function starts' -- and an inferred endpoint is both a correctness risk and unreadable in review, because the call says 1983 to 2050 rather than what it meant.

Proposed: --range-start-match and --range-end-before-match (regex or exact, resolved server-side, refusing when a match is absent or ambiguous), and where the repository is indexed, --symbol <name> resolving to that item's whole extent. Both make the intent explicit in the request and remove the arithmetic.

This is the ergonomic layer over T110's span token rather than a competitor: the token is the safe primitive, an anchor is how a caller names a span it has not read yet, and both eliminate the same class of mistake from different directions.
tasks.note: Ambiguity must refuse rather than pick the first match, for the reason the grep gate exists: a silent first-match is how a sweep edits the wrong occurrence and reports success.

tasks.title: Bump actions/checkout off the Node 20 deprecation, deliberately rather than blind
tasks.detail:
Every CI run now warns: "Node.js 20 is deprecated. The following actions target Node.js 20 but are being forced to run on Node.js 24: actions/checkout@v4." The workflow pins @v4 in six places (ci.yml lines 41, 268, 451, 552, 1088, 1143, 1164).

Nothing is broken today -- the runner forces v4 onto Node 24 and it works -- so this is noise removal and future-proofing, not a fix. That is exactly why it should NOT ride along with an unrelated urgent change: the current release is v7.0.1, so the move is v4 -> v7 across three major versions, and a checkout behaviour change (fetch depth defaults, submodule handling, credential persistence) would surface as a confusing failure in whatever PR happened to carry it.

Do it on its own branch: read the v5, v6 and v7 release notes for breaking changes, bump all six together, and watch a full matrix run. The register-branch and installer-build legs both depend on checkout behaviour, so a green run on one leg is not enough.
tasks.note: Raised by Tschallacka pasting the runner warning during the CI hang investigation. Deliberately deferred rather than bundled: the hang fix needed to land without carrying an unrelated risk.

tasks.title: At verbosity 0 the framing costs more than the answer
tasks.detail:
Measured 2026-09-08: a two-line read at verbosity 0 puts 32 bytes of file content into a 303-byte wire frame. The content is 10 percent of what crosses.

The rest is structure, and it is charged twice. Each response carries byte_count, request_id, sequence, type and version, and then a SECOND frame arrives whose whole content is request_id, result_generation, sequence, type and version to say the first one finished. For a single-frame answer that second frame is pure overhead.

Worth considering, in order of value and risk: omit the completion frame when the answer is a single non-streamed frame and nothing is paged; drop byte_count at level 0, since the transport already frames the message; and shorten or omit request_id where the adapter generates it and nothing correlates on it.

Note the ordering against the tab-id entry: a short tab id is the bigger single win and carries no protocol risk, so do that first and re-measure. This entry is only worth acting on if the framing still dominates afterwards -- at a 2-character id the frame is 241 bytes for the same 32 bytes of content, so it probably still does.

Keep the level contract intact whatever is trimmed: an out-of-range level is refused by name rather than clamped, capabilities and resources stay exempt, and a refusal keeps its full code, message and recovery choices at every level. Verbosity may never make an error harder to read.
tasks.note:
Split from the tab-id entry deliberately: id length and framing overhead are different mechanisms, and fixing either leaves the other.

SHARPER RULE (Tschallacka): level 0 must not repeat what the caller already sent. The tab id is the clearest case -- it came in on the request, so echoing it back is pure repetition -- and the principle is general: at level 0 return the ANSWER, not a restatement of the question.

The one case that must survive, from protocol.md: a request names its tab in FOUR ways -- by tab_id, by tab_path, by file path, or by naming nothing at all, which means the sessions focused tab. Only the first of those makes the id redundant. A caller that named a FILE, or named nothing, has no id yet, so the answering tabs id is new information and must still be returned or the caller has no handle for next time. And a response from a DIFFERENT tab than the one addressed must always name it, which is the property T98 exists for: a refused call never moves the focus, so the tab that answered a refusal is not the tab the caller meant.

So: omit tab_id when the caller supplied it and the answering tab is that same tab; include it otherwise.

Note on this entry itself -- the first version of this note lost the word "file" to a shell command substitution, because backticks inside a double-quoted argument run as a command. Same trap recorded in T115. Register text takes single quotes, or no backticks at all.

tasks.title: Mark a review rationale superseded when a later cycle replaces it
tasks.detail: codex postmortem recommendation 6. The Verdict rationale is a single field rewritten by hand each cycle; across four cycles here I replaced it four times, and nothing would have flagged it had I forgotten. A stale rationale is worse than an absent one because it reads as current: it names findings by id and asserts a verdict that the findings table may already contradict. Either stamp the rationale with the cycle it was written for and warn when the archived cycle count moves past it, or fold the rationale into the same helper that rewrites the findings table.
tasks.blocked_on: the review-document format owner: needs a rationale-cycle stamp written when the rationale is written (see note)
tasks.note: Attempted and reverted, deliberately. I built the staleness signal on the archived cycle number and it does not carry the meaning the entry assumed: archive 'Cycle N' names the state BEFORE run N, while a rationale saying 'Cycle N' names the review cycle whose findings just landed. Measured on a fixture — after two update runs the archive holds Cycle 1 and Cycle 2 while the rationale legitimately still reads Cycle 1 — so a warning keyed on the difference fires on the normal path, which is the T67 failure I had just fixed elsewhere. Correcting for the off-by-one then made it silent on the real case. B44 records that the numbering breaks after gaps and is closed as not-a-defect, so the counter is not a sound basis for this and no arithmetic on it will be. What would work is a stamp recording which cycle a rationale describes, written when the rationale is written rather than inferred from prose — that is a review-document format change and belongs with whoever owns the format. Reverted rather than shipping a warning that misfires in both directions.

tasks.title: Decide what a converted test prints on success
tasks.detail: DECIDED — t_end adopted, matching the 42 tests already using it, so byte-identical stdout is not the acceptance criterion. `t_end` prints `<test>: PASS`, or `<test>: N failure(s).` and exits 1. The three T1a tests print their own success line today, so adopting the library changes their stdout. Two defensible answers: adopt `t_end` and match the 42 tests that already use it, or keep each test's existing success line and call only the finding-recording part of the library. This has to be settled before T1a, because it decides the acceptance criterion: with `t_end`, byte-identical stdout cannot be the test of a correct conversion, and the proof has to compare the *findings* instead. **Common to T1a-T1c.** Not every `exit` is a finding: a missing fixture or an absent `openssl` is a precondition and must keep exiting. Conversion changes *when* a test stops, so later assertions begin running against state a fail-fast run never reached — that can surface real failures or hit setup that assumed the abort. Prove each one the way the earlier batch of 26 was proved: capture stdout, stderr and exit code before and after, diff them, and confirm the test still fails when an assertion is broken. Counts measured by brace-matching each reporter's own body, not by an awk range: `/^(fail|note_fail)\(\)/,/^}/` runs past a one-line `fail() { …; }` into the next function and finds *its* `exit`, which is how this file came to claim 18 fail-fast tests when there are 6. 42 tests already accumulate via `t_record`/`t_fail`; 15 define no reporter at all and are out of scope here.

tasks.title: Give editor responses a verbosity contract, so a two-line edit does not cost a screen of JSON
tasks.detail:
Michael, 2026-09-07: 'the json response given back is very very verbose. Is there a way to limit it to the essential feedback if any, with a flag in the mcp/binary for verbosity? no flag: just status good, status bad, with option to get more data. with verbosity 1, just some data useful for verification/next step. with verbosity 2, more data useful for navigating, verbosity 3, all data as it is now' and 'editing two lines, getting 15 lines or more json back seems wasteful of tokens'.

MEASURED on this machine, build tree client at bin/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl:
- open of a TWO-LINE file: 1199 bytes, 47 lines. Carries a four-field resources block, a 64-char server_generation, a 64-char tab_uuid, a session_token, index_coverage, and both envelope frames - on every open.
- insert of one word: 378 bytes, 25 lines, whose entire actionable content is revision 1 and dirty true.

The cost lands on the MCP surface hardest: every response is context an agent pays for on every edit, so response shape is a token budget, not a formatting preference.

THE LADDER AS SPECIFIED (Michael's own levels, to be honoured rather than reinterpreted):
- no flag / level 0: status good or status bad, and nothing else, with a documented way to ask for more.
- level 1: what verification and the next step need - revision, dirty, and a refusal code when bad.
- level 2: level 1 plus what navigation needs - cursors, coordinates, completeness and paging keys.
- level 3: everything, exactly the current payload, so nothing regresses for a caller that wants it all.

DESIGN CONSTRAINTS to settle before coding:
- Level 0 must still let a mutating caller learn the new revision, or it breaks the revision-guard contract that every mutation depends on (SKILL.md agent responsibility 5). Either revision counts as status, or level 1 is the floor for mutations - decide and document which.
- open is the response that seeds a session: session_token, endpoint identity and tab_uuid are how a client reconnects. Trimming those at a low level must not break reconnection, so open's floor may differ from a mutation's.
- The default matters more than the flag. If level 3 stays the default, nothing improves for an agent that does not know the flag exists; if the default drops, protocol.md's documented response shapes all change and every consumer must be checked.
- resources on every open looks like the single cheapest win: it answers a question (can I afford a rewrite) that has its own read-only resources command.
- Wants a scope-and-decide pass before implementation - this touches every response shape, protocol.md, the man page, the MCP tool schemas and the capabilities command.
tasks.note:
Filed as a todo rather than a bug deliberately: it is new capability with a specified design, not promised behaviour that fails. Recommend it as its OWN PR after the eleven-bug batch merges - folding a cross-cutting response-shaping change into a bug batch would make both hard to review, and B217/B226 are already moving the MCP schema. Raised by Michael on the chat bus while a peer session was driving the installed MCP editor. REFS: this entry should carry src/ai-text-editor/src/verbosity.rs, src/ai-text-editor/src/bin/ai-text-editor-server.rs, src/ai-text-editor-mcp/src/lib.rs and ai-text-editor/references/protocol.md. They are recorded here in prose because they cannot be recorded properly: `todo update` has no --refs and --touching matches refs alone, so `todo list --touching ai-text-editor` misses this entry and nothing shipped can fix it. Filed as B260. IMPLEMENTED on feat/t99-verbosity-ladder (674f532a), awaiting merge. Measured, same two-line file and client as the before-numbers above: open 1226 -> 624 bytes at the default (49% off), 310 at level 0; insert 523 -> 439 (16%), 310 at level 0. Opens halve and mutations do not - a mutations floor is what the revision contract and B226/B230 require it to report, and the remaining bulk is the two pretty-printed envelope frames rather than the payload. Default is level 1 not 0, a deliberate deviation from the specification: level 0 cannot carry a revision and every mutations guard requires one, so a level-0 default would silently break the revision contract. Level 0 stays reachable explicitly. Per-KEY tier table rather than per-verb, because a per-verb key list is what B237 was. Three rules the levels do not bend: every level carries the verbs own result and names its tab, a refusal is never trimmed, and capabilities/resources are exempt. The tiers were re-derived from SKILL.mds own agent responsibilities after a first pass contradicted them - the three tab-state flags and completeness/result-generation are named there as obligations, so a ladder that drops them is not terse, it is in breach - and four further keys moved up on the same argument once the suite showed what the default was withholding: a searchs pager_key and count, a bounded reads start_line/end_line/returned_bytes, an indexs granularity, and a zero-result searchs note (B218 is the cost of not having that last one). Already shipped; this entry was stale. Verified live through the MCP on 2026-09-08: the same two-line read returns 121 bytes at verbosity 0 (tab_id and text only) and 216 at verbosity 3 (adding revision, dirty, disk_diverged, complete, start_line, end_line).

What exists: src/ai-text-editor/src/verbosity.rs with DEFAULT_VERBOSITY 1, MAX_VERBOSITY 3, tier(), requested(), apply() and verb_is_exempt(); the server validates the level and refuses one outside 0..=3 by NAME rather than clamping; capabilities and resources are exempt because their payload is metadata by definition; and a refusal keeps its full code, message and recovery choices at every level, so turning verbosity down cannot hide an error. The MCP adapter carries it on every tool with the ladder described, and deliberately not as an ADAPTER_ARGUMENTS entry -- the server consumes it, so it stays in the payload like file and tab_id.

tasks.title: One client session owns the connection: the tail serves send/read over a control socket
tasks.detail:
Tschallacka's ruling on B283: reading and sending must use the same client session. The tail becomes the session's owner -- it holds the single TLS connection and is the only cursor writer -- and serves send, read, names, join and leave over a control socket in the session state dir. Those verbs look for that socket first: if it answers they forward the request, block for the reply, and print what the owner reports from the wire; if it is absent or stale they behave as they do today and open their own connection, so nothing regresses where no tail runs.

CONCURRENCY (Tschallacka's ruling): the socket gets its OWN monitor thread. It owns the listener, accepts a connection, reads the request, and pings the main process atomically that an action is waiting -- the tail loop is never blocked by socket I/O, and a slow or dead client cannot stall the bus. Shape, std only, no new crates: a Mutex<VecDeque<Request>> for the queue plus an AtomicBool set with Release on push and read with Acquire in the loop, so the main thread pays one atomic load per iteration and takes the lock only when there is something to take. Each Request carries an mpsc::Sender for its reply; the monitor thread blocks on recv and writes the answer back to the client, so the blocking is always on the monitor side. A recv timeout makes the monitor answer 'owner busy, retry' itself rather than leaving a client hanging -- an unanswered send must never look delivered.

Lifecycle: the monitor thread watches a shutdown AtomicBool so QUIT ends it, and only the socket inode this process created is unlinked. If the monitor thread dies the tail keeps tailing and the socket is removed, so clients fall back to their own connection instead of hanging on a dead socket. Requests are served in arrival order and a send is written between whole lines, never interleaved into a partial one.

The precedent is in this repo twice: interactive-shell is a long-lived process owning a PTY with a short-lived input client over a 0600 socket in a 0700 directory, and ai-text-editor is a server owning document state with a short-lived client, whose SessionRecord (endpoint, pid, start_time_ns, server_generation, session_token) is already the stale-owner design this needs -- a pid alone is reused, so it is paired with the start time and a takeover is explicit. Windows has no unix socket, so it takes loopback TCP with a token, as ai-text-editor does. --no-session must bypass the socket entirely, since it means do not touch shared state. Message splitting stays in the owner, where wire_segments already lives.
tasks.note: Closes B283 by construction rather than by patch: with one owner the server never sees a second connection under the nick, so it never suffixes one. B254 and B269 become structurally impossible for the same reason -- the process that reads the stream is the only process that writes the cursor. Landed on unix 2026-09-08 (commit 8e4b52e0, PR 78): control.rs holds the socket, the monitor thread and the client-side forwarder; lib.rs gained the serve_* verbs, the owner setup in tail, and forward_or_fall_back in send/read/names/join/leave. Ten unit tests plus chat/tests/test-chat-owner-socket.sh, whose --no-session control is the permanent mutation proving the unsuffixed assertion is not vacuous. Windows is NOT covered and is now T111; there the cfg(not(unix)) arm returns None so every verb keeps its pre-T107 behaviour. Two register entries came out of the work: B294 (insert refuses a line number read accepts) and B295 (the remote read arm saves a mention cursor), and B295 is why serve_read copies the remote behaviour rather than the better local one.

tasks.title: The revision guard must be advertised as the preferred edit guard, above expected_text
tasks.detail:
Tschallacka's point, 2026-09-08: re-sending expected_text on every replace is OUTPUT tokens, while re-reading a span to learn it is INPUT tokens, and input is the cheaper half by a wide margin. The revision guard already proves the property that matters for a span located at the current revision -- the document has not moved since the read the line numbers came from -- so for that case expected_text is duplicated generation with no added safety.

The two guards answer different questions and both must stay: revision proves the DOCUMENT is unchanged, expected_text proves the BYTES AT THIS SPAN are the ones meant. The second earns its cost only when the span's coordinates could be stale or computed -- a line number carried across the agent's own edits, a search result from an earlier revision, an offset derived by arithmetic. It is not the default.

What to change: SKILL.md and references/protocol.md currently present expected_text as the content guard without ranking the two or naming the cost, so an agent reaches for it by default and pays output tokens per edit. State the preference explicitly -- read, then guard by revision; add expected_text only when the coordinates did not come from a read at that same revision -- and say why in the token terms above, since that is the reason and an agent that does not know it will keep paying. The capabilities command should carry the same ordering, since that is what an agent queries rather than the prose.
tasks.note: Merged as PR #91 (b59dfc7), squash-merged to master. SKILL.md and references/protocol.md state the guard preference explicitly in token terms; capabilities now advertises guard_preference: {order, expected_text_when} so an agent can query it rather than depend on the prose. Verified locally against the real built binary (tests/test-ai-text-editor.sh, which stays UNCONFIGURED in CI since CI never populates the per-skill bin dir); full CI green on PR #91.

tasks.title: leave stops the tail on that channel, and a tail follows a set of channels
tasks.detail:
Tschallacka's ruling, 2026-09-08: a leave on a channel must STOP the tail on that channel, not refuse. T107 shipped the refusal -- serve_leave answered 64 with 'stop the tail to leave it' -- which is the wrong end of the choice: the caller asked to leave and should be obeyed.

The two halves are one change. 'The tail on that channel' cannot mean one tail per channel: there is one owner per session and only one tail holds the control socket, so a leave aimed at a second channel could never reach a second tail. So a tail follows a SET of channels: --chan is repeatable, each channel keeps its own cursor (the session already holds a map), the loop prints any followed channel, and the LASTID resync walks the set one channel per tick so bookkeeping does not grow with the count.

leave then means: PART the channel, drop its cursor, drop it from the set -- and if the set is now empty the tail stops, because a tail following nothing would otherwise hold a connection subscribed to nothing while still answering as the session's owner.

This also closes B296 by construction: a forwarded join ADDS to the set, so a channel the owner is a member of is a channel the tail prints. Membership and listening stop being able to diverge.
tasks.note: Raised as a question about whether a tail can follow several channels; the answer was no, and the ruling makes it yes because the leave semantics require it. Landed d7c12ec5 on PR 78. --chan is repeatable; each channel keeps its own cursor; the loop prints any followed channel; the LASTID resync walks the set one channel per tick so bookkeeping does not grow with the count; tail --local refuses a second --chan rather than quietly following the first. leave parts a channel, drops its cursor and drops it from the set, and stops the tail when the set empties. Closed B296 by construction. Documented in chat/SKILL.md (d6e54af8) including why a second tail is the thing to avoid -- flowchart measured nick/nick-2 across two tails on the bus.

tasks.title: Give run-tests.sh a per-test timeout and the CI jobs a timeout-minutes
tasks.detail:
There is no timeout anywhere: run_one has none, and ci.yml declares no timeout-minutes on any job, so every job inherits GitHub 6-hour default. Measured 2026-09-08: three test-suite legs sat in_progress for over three hours on one PR while every build leg had long since passed, and the only signal was the absence of a result.

Two changes. run_one wraps each test in the timeout(1) utility, so a hang FAILS AS ITSELF and names the test rather than silently consuming the leg -- report it distinctly (exit 124) so a timeout is never mistaken for an assertion failure. And each suite job gets a timeout-minutes as the backstop for a hang outside a test.

The per-test timeout is the one that matters: it converts "the leg never finished" into "test-X timed out after N seconds", which is the difference between a three-hour mystery and a two-minute diagnosis.
tasks.note: Already done — implemented directly by the maintainer in efa4a18 (2026-09-08, on master before this session started), triggered by a real 3-hour CI hang. run_one wraps each test in timeout(1) (test_timeout_seconds, default 600s, AI_SKILLS_TEST_TIMEOUT override), missing timeout(1) degrades with a printed notice rather than failing the runner, exit 124 is reported as its own TIMEOUT outcome distinct from FAIL. ci.yml's test and test-bash32 jobs both carry timeout-minutes: 45. Verified: efa4a18 is an ancestor of master; a deliberately hanging test under AI_SKILLS_TEST_TIMEOUT=2 exits 124 as expected.

tasks.title: Let todo and bugs read note and detail text from a file, so prose never crosses shell quoting
tasks.detail:
Register prose can only reach the binaries through argv today. --file names the REGISTER, not the text, so every note and detail is a shell argument -- and a shell argument is where prose gets damaged.

Measured twice in one session, both silent: a note containing backticks ran them as command substitution, so one word became empty in T115 and another was replaced by the output of the file(1) utility in T119. Neither errored. Both wrote a register entry with a word missing, which is worse than a failure because the entry looks finished.

The workaround is single quotes, and the workaround is itself the evidence that the interface is wrong: prose in single quotes cannot contain an apostrophe, so the repaired T119 note had to be reworded around every possessive it wanted to use. Register prose should not be written around the shell.

Wanted: --note-file PATH and --detail-file PATH, and the same on bugs for --reproduce, --observed, --expected, --mechanism, --fix and --verification. Then the composition is the right one: the ai-text-editor writes the prose to a file, the binary reads the bytes verbatim, and nothing in between interprets them. A single dash meaning stdin serves the same purpose in a pipeline.

The register must still be WRITTEN by the binary, which owns the schema, stamps skill_version, and has a check() whose whole job is catching entries that did not come from the tools. This is about how the text reaches it, not about who writes the file.
tasks.note: Merged as PR #88 (46f33ef), squash-merged to master. All writable text fields on both todo and bugs now have a --<field>-file counterpart reading from a file or stdin (-); shared Args::resolve_file_flag kept byte-identical between the crates. 47+25 cargo tests, tests/test-register-file-flags.sh end-to-end through the built binaries (including the stdin path), full ./run-tests.sh green.

tasks.title: bump the GitHub Actions we pin to their latest majors, which run on node24
tasks.detail:
Every CI run prints 'Node 20 is being deprecated. This workflow is running with Node 24 by default.' We do not choose that: a JavaScript action declares its own runtime as runs.using in its action.yml, and the majors we pin declare node20. The punycode and url.parse DeprecationWarnings in the same logs come from inside those actions' bundled code under the newer Node, not from anything in this repo.

What we pin, and where it should go -- runs.using verified by reading each new major's action.yml directly, not from release notes:

  actions/checkout           v4 -> v7.0.1   node24
  actions/upload-artifact    v4 -> v7.0.1   node24
  actions/download-artifact  v4 -> v8.0.1   node24

Call sites: .github/workflows/ci.yml lines 627, 741, 863, 884, 909, 932, 987 and .github/workflows/render-artifacts.yml lines 30, 63. dtolnay/rust-toolchain@1.98 is a composite action and is not implicated.

This is NOT a find-and-replace. upload-artifact v4->v7 and download-artifact v4->v8 cross breaking changes in artifact naming and overwrite behaviour, and we depend on that behaviour: the rust-artifact-manifest job downloads the per-target artifacts by name and publishes their hashes. So the bump has to be proven by a CI run that exercises that round trip, and the manifest job is the assertion.

Do not reach for ACTIONS_ALLOW_USE_UNSECURE_NODE_VERSION=true. It silences the warning by pinning the runner to the deprecated runtime, which is the opposite of the fix and leaves us to discover the removal as a hard failure instead.

Urgency: the warnings are noise today and become failures when GitHub removes node20 from the runners (announced 2025-09-19). Raised by Tschallacka on 2026-09-04 after reading them in a run's logs.
tasks.note: Merged as PR #93 (a464bcb), squash-merged to master. actions/checkout v4->v7.0.1, actions/upload-artifact v4->v7.0.1, actions/download-artifact v4->v8.0.1, all verified node24 against the tag's own action.yml. Also bumped registers.yml/registers-sync.yml's checkout, not named in the original filing but in scope for 'every pinned major'. The rust-artifact-manifest job's upload/download-artifact round trip (the todo's own prescribed proof) passed on PR #93's CI, alongside one unrelated transient DNS flake on the macOS runner (dtolnay/rust-toolchain failing to resolve static.rust-lang.org) that a rerun cleared.

tasks.title: Every ai-text-editor action must be invokable on a tab id
tasks.detail: Verbs route today by file/endpoint/identity; the tab uuid is the stable handle the server already issues in every open answer. Every verb - read, search, insert, replace, save, close, cursor, the job verbs - should accept the tab id as the whole of its addressing, so a caller that holds an id never needs a path.
tasks.note: Already done - implemented directly by the maintainer in cde4138 ('ai-text-editor: address any tab by id or path, and carry a focused tab'), on master. Verified live against the real binary 2026-09-09: read AND a mutating verb (insert) both work addressed by --tab-id alone, no file/endpoint needed. Per the entry's own note, B261 (a live already-connected MCP agent can't see the new tab_id/tab_path schema until it restarts) is a separate, still-open concern about reachability for existing sessions, not about whether the feature itself works.

tasks.title: Tabs addressable by filename or partial workspace-root path; ambiguity returns a result set
tasks.detail: The recovery for an AI that forgot the tab id: pass a filename, or a partial path from the workspace root, and the resolver answers the single matching tab - or, when several tabs match, a result set of candidates with their tab ids rather than a guess or an error. Sequels naturally after T96, which gives the candidates their handle.
tasks.note: Already done - same commit as T96 (cde4138). Verified live: --tab-path with a bare filename resolves the single matching tab; with two tabs sharing that filename, the request is refused tab_ambiguous naming both candidates with their tab_ids rather than guessing.

tasks.title: A session carries a focused tab id; unmarked actions run on it
tasks.detail: Every session/identity tracks a focused tab. Any request with no file, endpoint, or tab marker is performed on the focused tab; open sets the focus, and every response names the tab it answered so a caller never writes to the wrong tab quietly. tasks.title: CODE-STYLE 11: say that an item inserted after a comment must not adopt it
tasks.detail:
Three instances of one edit shape in a day, each reported separately by the nitpicker: installer/src/36-ui-render.sh twice (iui_integration_offered inserted between iui_info_actions and its docblock, and the same on the pane actions) and src/chat-client-rs/src/lib.rs:2336 (four tests inserted between a B271 comment and the B271 test, so the comment now heads a B278 test and the described test has none).

Filed as B282, but the nitpicker's point is that three corrections are worse value than one rule: CODE-STYLE 11 already says a comment states a fact about the code it sits on, and what is missing is the editing rule that follows from it -- when you insert an item directly after a comment, the comment belongs to what was there before, so move your item below it or carry the comment with the thing it describes.

Cheap to enforce beyond prose: a check that a doc comment naming a symbol sits on a symbol of that name would have caught all three.
tasks.note: Closed by session_01KC83KhD4yu3j3AUGe3qeoi: fixed in CODE-STYLE.md §11 via PR #94, merged as bb2c4a1c.

tasks.title: CODE-STYLE 11 does not state a comment-length cap for a function-leading block
tasks.detail: Section 11 caps comment length, but both of its model citations are in-body comments. The block that sits immediately above a function definition -- where most comments in this repo actually are -- has no stated cap, so nobody can be corrected against it and nobody can comply with it deliberately. Decide the cap for that position and write it into the section, or state that the position is deliberately uncapped. Raised by the nitpicker as a proposal it explicitly refused to enforce as law, because enforcing an unwritten rule from an agent's notes teaches people to disregard the ones that are written.
tasks.note: Proposal, not law. T103 covers the orphan-comment rule and is a separate gap. Still open, and now wider: with CODE-STYLE governing every language (T106), the unwritten cap covers a Rust item's /// block as well as a shell function-leading one. Section 11 now says plainly that the three-line limit is written for IN-BODY comments, that an item's leading block is therefore uncapped, and that this is not permission to narrate -- the content rules still bind it. That is a holding position, not a ruling: the question this entry asks, whether a leading block should be capped at all and at what length, is unchanged. Closed by session_01KC83KhD4yu3j3AUGe3qeoi: fixed in CODE-STYLE.md §11 via PR #94, merged as bb2c4a1c.

tasks.title: There is no comment contract for Rust, only for shell
tasks.detail: CODE-STYLE opens with "every shell file", so its comment rules -- density, placement, length, no dev-journey prose -- formally cover none of the Rust crates, which are now most of the code in the repository. Every Rust comment correction made so far has been by analogy rather than by rule. Either widen the contract's scope to say it applies to every source file whatever the language, naming the few rules that are shell-specific, or write a Rust section beside it. Raised by the nitpicker as a proposal it explicitly refused to enforce as law.
tasks.note:
Proposal, not law. Peer of T105: that one is a gap inside a rule, this is a gap in the contract's scope. RULED by Tschallacka, 2026-09-08: widen it. 'We started with bash only, so we evolved to rust focussed to get around system limitations etc... So widen it, so it applies to all languages. they are good rules, that should be held globally.'

So the shell-only scope was an artefact of shell being all there was when the rules were written, never a judgement that Rust deserved fewer.
